floors.content: What is a line? Take a stick. Drag it through wet sand. You have made a groove. That groove is a line. Yes — it is a line.
A railway line. Is that a line? A phone line. A help line. The word shows up everywhere. And underneath all of them is the same idea: a straight path from one place to another.
In mathematics a line is defined as a straight one-dimensional figure that has no thickness and extends infinitely in both directions.

You would call that groove a line. I would too. If you pick up a pencil and draw a straight mark on a sheet of paper, you have made a line. A crease in a folded sheet, a crack in a wall — we call all of these lines. They begin somewhere. They end somewhere. That is what the word means, for most of us, most of the time.

Euclid meant something else. Around 300 BC he wrote down a definition that has lasted twenty-three centuries: a line is breadthless length. No thickness at all. And it never starts and it never stops. A Euclidian line goes on forever in both directions.

You cannot hold a Euclidian line. You cannot draw one — the page runs out before the line does. A crack quits at the edge of the brick. None of these are what Euclid meant.

We built on it anyway. For two thousand years people have used this thing nobody has ever seen to do things you can see.

The sand groove was never the line. The line was the idea it pointed to.
